name: Borosilicate glass bed
summary: A rigid heat-resistant glass sheet clamped or bolted over the heater — the flattest common build surface and the reason it survives as an upgrade long after flexible steel took over. It is rigid, so every print comes off by cold release and a scraper rather than by flexing, and most materials want a glue-stick or hairspray layer on top of the bare glass.
surface_makeup: Borosilicate glass (boron trioxide plus silica), chosen over ordinary soda-lime or picture-frame glass for low thermal expansion and much better thermal-shock resistance. Used bare, or with an applied adhesion layer (glue stick, hairspray, PVA-based sprays), or in a 'matte'/carborundum variant where a silica-carbide texture is fired onto the glass surface. Chemically inert and dimensionally stable, with no coating to degrade.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: glue stick or hairspray on bare glass
filament_compatibility.notes: Bare borosilicate can be too slick for PLA on its own; a thin PVA glue-stick film is the standard fix and also gives the glossy bottom finish glass is prized for.
Same as base PLA; the mirror-smooth glass bottom pairs well with silk's sheen.
Abrasive fills are a non-issue for glass — there is no coating for filler particles to score.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: glue stick REQUIRED as a release layer
filament_compatibility.notes: The classic glass hazard: PETG bonds chemically to bare glass and can pull a conchoidal chip out of the plate on removal. Glue stick is used here as a barrier, not for grip.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: hairspray, glue stick, or ABS slurry
filament_compatibility.notes: Glass takes ABS bed temps without complaint; the difficulty is warp, not the surface. ABS/acetone slurry is a traditional glass-specific adhesion trick.
Same as ABS. On a rigid plate a lifted corner cannot be rescued by flexing, so use a brim and an enclosure.

filament_compatibility.notes: Not well documented for bare glass in the sources; nylon adhesion aids are discussed for PEI and garolite instead. Nylon on bare glass is generally reported as unreliable — use the adhesive layer.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: Magigoo PC or glue stick required

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: PP adhesion promoter or packing tape over the glass
filament_compatibility.notes: Not covered in glass sources. PP will not stick to bare glass; the traditional workaround is taping PP packing tape to the plate so PP prints onto its own polymer.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: PP adhesion promoter or packing tape
filament_compatibility.notes: Same as PP; undocumented for glass.

filament_compatibility.adhesion_aid: none (PVA is itself the usual glass adhesive)
filament_compatibility.notes: Not covered in sources. PVA sticks to glass readily — the risk is the opposite one, residue left behind that goes tacky in humid air. Wash the plate after PVA contact.
Undocumented; treated as PVA-equivalent, and normally only touches the plate as a support interface.

Not covered in sources. PEEK needs 130-160 C beds and a heated chamber; the glass itself would cope but no adhesion route on glass is documented and the thermal-shock risk in a hot chamber cycle is real.

preparation: Before the first print, wash the plate thoroughly with dish soap and warm water or a glass cleaner to strip the oils and manufacturing residue that come on new glass, then dry it fully — a fingerprint on glass is far more disruptive than on a textured surface because there is no mechanical key to fall back on. Most users then apply an adhesion layer, because bare borosilicate is genuinely too slick for reliable first layers with many materials: a thin, even glue-stick film (crosshatched and smoothed with a damp cloth) or a light hairspray/PVA spray coat, applied cold and off to the side so overspray does not reach the rails. Reapply every few prints or whenever you see the layer going patchy. Level carefully once and enjoy the payoff — glass is the flattest surface in common use, so mesh compensation has very little to correct. Bring the bed up to temperature gradually rather than slamming it to 110 C from cold; borosilicate resists thermal shock far better than window glass but it is still glass, and a clamp point plus a fast ramp is how plates crack.
cleaning: Routine cleaning is easy because there is no coating to protect: wipe the cold plate with IPA or a glass cleaner such as Windex to lift oils and old adhesive haze. For a deep clean, take the plate off the printer and wash it in the sink with dish soap and warm water, using a plastic scrubber to work off caked glue stick, then dry it completely before remounting — water trapped under a clamped plate will steam on the next heat cycle. Because glass is hard and chemically inert you can use a razor blade at a shallow angle to shave off welded plastic, which is a genuine advantage over coated surfaces, though it is also the most common way people chip an edge. What to avoid: rapid heat/cold cycling of any kind (a cold wet cloth on a hot plate is the fastest way to crack one), aggressive levering with a metal blade, and dropping or knocking the edges. Acetone is essentially harmless to plain borosilicate itself, but this is unverified in the sources and it will attack any fired-on or applied coating on a matte/carborundum variant, so keep it off textured glass.
model_removal: Cold release, always. Let the bed cool completely to room temperature and differential contraction between the plastic and the glass breaks most of the bond on its own — with PLA on a glue-stick layer, prints frequently release with an audible tick as the plate cools, before you touch anything. For the rest, work a thin scraper, spatula or razor blade under a corner at a shallow angle and lift gradually. The thing that makes glass different from every flexible surface in this catalog is that you cannot flex it: there is no popping the sheet to shear the bond, so removal force is always applied by a tool at the perimeter. That makes patience the main technique — prying a warm print, or attacking it from the center, is how both prints and plates get destroyed. If the plate is clamped, remove it from the printer first so you are not levering against the bed springs or the clamps.
stuck_print_recovery: Work up the escalation ladder and stop at the first success. Give it more time first — a plate that is merely warm still holds. Then run IPA around the perimeter and let capillary action pull it under the first layer; this is the highest-yield trick on glass because the bond line is flat and continuous. For large flat parts, slide dental floss or fishing line under one edge and saw it back and forth along the bond line, which distributes force instead of concentrating it at a corner. Next, try a heat-then-cool cycle: bring the bed back to printing temperature to soften the interface, then let it cool fully again, which often releases a part that had cooled unevenly. A freezer trip of 10-15 minutes does work on glass, but it is riskier here than with flexible steel because you are thermally shocking a brittle plate — take it off the printer, let it reach room temperature first, and accept the crack risk. Escalate to a plastic spatula worked in from a corner, and only then to a razor blade held nearly flat. Never use a sharp metal tool driven under the center of a print, never hammer, and never pour cold water on a hot plate.
lifespan_notes: Effectively unlimited service life in normal use, and that is the main argument for glass: there is no coating to wear out, no powder coat to polish smooth, and no adhesion decay curve to track. Failure is binary rather than gradual — the plate cracks or chips and gets replaced. The usual causes are thermal shock (fast ramps, cold liquid on a hot plate, freezer recovery attempts), impact, over-tightened clamps, and razor-blade removal that catches an edge. PETG bonding to bare glass deserves its own mention as a lifespan issue: the print can take a shell-shaped flake of glass with it, permanently pitting the plate, which is why the glue-stick barrier is non-negotiable for copolyesters. There is no recoating or refurbishment path; a damaged plate is replaced outright, though at $15-30 that is a mild outcome compared with replacing a coated steel sheet.

price.notes: ~250 mm class. 235-250 mm Amazon/AliExpress plates commonly $18-25; branded larger formats (e.g. 250x320 mm) around $30 and up. Textured carborundum/matte variants sit at the upper end.

additional_notes: Not compatible with magnetic quick-swap systems — the plate is rigid and gets bolted or binder-clipped onto an aluminum heat spreader, so you cannot pop it off mid-workflow the way you can with a spring-steel sheet. It is also single-surface: there are no double-sided glass plates, unlike Prusa's satin/smooth/textured steel sheets. Historically important as the pre-PEI default — original Prusa i3 MK2-era machines ran heated glass with hairspray or 3DLac-style PVA sprays before the move to PEI sheets on the MK2.5/MK3, and Creality still ships and sells glass for the Ender-3 class. Bambu Lab does not offer a glass option at all. The lasting reason to choose it is first-layer consistency: glass is flatter than any steel sheet, which shows up directly in large-footprint first layers, and it gives a mirror-gloss part bottom that no textured surface can.

provenance.conflicts: No source quantifies a thermal-shock rating or maximum surface temperature for the glass; the 150 C figure recorded here is a conservative practical ceiling reflecting that borosilicate comfortably exceeds any FDM bed temperature (120 C+) while the real constraint is the heater and adhesive beneath it, not the glass. Sources caution generally against acetone on coated surfaces but do not state whether acetone is safe on plain borosilicate — recorded as probably harmless on bare glass, unsafe on matte/carborundum coatings, both unverified. Nylon (all grades), PP, PVA/BVOH and high-temperature materials are not covered for glass in any source; those rows are extrapolated from general material behavior and adjacent-surface guidance. TPU bed temperature on glass specifically is unverified. Whether the freezer trick is acceptable on borosilicate is genuinely disputed in community practice: it works, but it is a deliberate thermal shock of a brittle plate.
